Notable examples include RCA AR-1264 (1929). This record is the front door of the database: start here, then follow the teaching ladder from the simple definition (record 2) through the engineering deep-dives (records 4–6) to the advanced restoration and collecting guides.

title: What Is Theremin? — Definition
body:
Audio recording is capturing sound for later playback: Edison's phonograph cylinders (1877), Berliner's discs, electrical recording, magnetic tape and wire, vinyl LPs, cassettes, 8-tracks, DAT, MiniDisc, and the playback machines — phonographs, reel-to-reels, turntables, Walkmans — that carried music into daily life before digital files.

In the context of this database, the Theremin is presented as one audio history record among the audio recording history family. 1920's touchless: hands in electric fields — the eerie voice of sci-fi.

title: Origins and History of Theremin
body:
The Theremin belongs to the 1920–present era and traces to Leon Theremin.

Edison shouted 'Mary had a little lamb' into a phonograph in 1877; cylinders ruled until Berliner's disc (1887) proved cheaper to stamp. Electrical recording (1925) and microphones replaced horns; 78s gave way to the LP (Columbia, 1948) and 45 (RCA, 1949). Valdemar Poulsen's telegraphone (1898) pioneered magnetic recording; German Magnetophons and Ampex (1948) made tape the studio standard. Philips' Compact Cassette (1963) democratized recording; the Walkman (1979) privatized listening. The CD (1982) began the digital endgame, but vinyl never fully died — and cassettes came back as culture.

Within that longer story, Theremin: The RCA Theremin (1929); Clara Rockmore's virtuosity. The theremin is the original electronic instrument.

title: How Theremin Works
body:
Acoustic recording cut grooves directly with a horn-driven diaphragm. Electrical recording uses a microphone, amplifier, and cutter head (disc) or record head (tape). Tape stores sound as magnetic patterns on oxide; bias (high-frequency AC) linearizes the response. Discs are read by a stylus tracing the groove, generating tiny voltages in a cartridge (magnetic or crystal), equalized by the RIAA curve. Cassettes run 1-7/8 ips tape past heads in a pocket shell; 8-tracks loop endlessly on 1/4-inch tape with a moving head selecting programs.

Applied to the Theremin (1920–present, Leon Theremin): The theremin is the original electronic instrument.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Theremin — Components
body:
Every Theremin is an assembly of the audio recording history family's standard parts:

• Cutter head / stylus — Cuts or traces the groove.
• Cartridge — MM, MC, ceramic — turns stylus motion into signal.
• Tonearm — Pivoted or linear-tracking arm holding the cartridge.
• Platter & motor — Belt, idler, or direct drive at 33/45/78.
• Tape head — Record, playback, erase heads in the tape path.
• Capstan & pinch roller — Precision speed control of tape.
• Bias oscillator — Ultrasonic AC linearizing tape response.
• Dolby / dbx — Noise reduction companding systems.
• Speaker / headphones — The final transducer.
• Amplifier — Tube then solid-state; the muscle.

When examining a surviving Theremin, identify these parts in order: Cutter head / stylus, Cartridge, Tonearm, Platter & motor, Tape head, Capstan & pinch roller.

title: Audio Recording History — Historical Timeline
body:
Milestones in the history of audio recording history:

• 1877 — Edison's phonograph: 'Mary had a little lamb'.
• 1887 — Berliner's disc gramophone patent.
• 1925 — Electrical recording replaces acoustic horns.
• 1948/1949 — LP (Columbia) and 45 (RCA) launch the format war's peace.
• 1948 — Ampex Model 200: tape enters US studios.
• 1963 — Philips Compact Cassette introduced.
• 1979 — Sony Walkman TPS-L2: music goes personal.
• 1982 — Compact Disc launches; digital begins.
• 1987 — DAT: digital tape for consumers (controversially).
• 1992 — MiniDisc and DCC: the last physical-format battle.

The Theremin (1920–present) sits on this timeline at: 1920's touchless: hands in electric fields — the eerie voice of sci-fi..

title: Key Figures Behind Audio Recording History
body:
The people who made audio recording history possible:

• Thomas Edison (1847–1931) — Phonograph 1877; the recording industry's founder.
• Emile Berliner (1851–1929) — Disc record and gramophone; lateral-cut grooves.
• Valdemar Poulsen (1869–1942) — Magnetic recording pioneer (telegraphone, 1898).

Theremin originates with Leon Theremin, standing on the work of the figures above.

title: Audio Recording History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of audio recording history:

• RIAA EQ — Standard record/playback equalization curve.
• wow & flutter — Slow/fast speed variations; the turntable/tape spec.
• ips — Inches per second: 15/7.5 studio, 3.75/1.875 consumer.
• NAB / IEC — Tape equalization standards.
• bias — Ultrasonic signal making tape recording linear.
• print-through — Magnetic ghosting between tape layers.
• tracking force — Stylus downforce, grams; too much wears records.
• anti-skate — Counteracts inward tonearm pull.
• azimuth — Head/groove alignment angle.
• head gap — Determines high-frequency response; smaller = better.
• Type I/II/IV — Ferric, chrome, metal cassette formulations.
• C-60/C-90 — Cassette lengths in minutes; thinner tape for longer.

title: Theremin in Culture
body:
Recording froze performance in time: Caruso in every parlor, then Ellington, Elvis, the Beatles — the 20th century has a soundtrack because grooves and tape kept it. The mixtape was a love letter; the Walkman made the city a movie with your score; the 8-track was road-trip furniture. Vinyl's ritual — sleeve, stylus drop, side flip — outlived every 'replacement'.

The Theremin carries that cultural charge directly: The theremin is the original electronic instrument.

title: Collecting and Preserving Theremin
body:
78s are heavy shellac — handle by edges, store vertically. First-press LPs in clean sleeves hold value; clean with proper fluid and brush. Reel-to-reel decks need belts and head checks; buy with original NAB hubs. Walkmans: belts and pinch rollers perish; Discmans: lasers weaken. Test Dolby calibration with a known tape.

For the Theremin specifically: 1920's touchless: hands in electric fields — the eerie voice of sci-fi.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working Theremin with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: Theremin Restoration Guide
body:
Demagnetize heads; clean tape path with isopropyl. Replace belts and idler tires. Check turntable speed with a strobe disc. Recap amplifiers. Store tape tails-out, vertical, cool and dry; bake sticky-shed tapes before playing.

Restoration order for a Theremin: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical audio history record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Theremin — Tape-time + RIAA/vinyl math (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes playing time from tape length and speed, groove pitch basics, and the RIAA time constants — the arithmetic of analog audio.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Theremin so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Analog audio math: tape time, vinyl sides, RIAA (public-domain formulas)
def tape_time_minutes(length_ft, ips):
    return length_ft * 12 / ips / 60

for ips, label in [(15, "studio 15ips"), (7.5, "reel 7.5ips"),
                   (3.75, "reel 3.75ips"), (1.875, "cassette")]:
    print(f"1800ft reel at {label}: {tape_time_minutes(1800, ips):.0f} min")

# Vinyl: ~ LP side at 33rpm, groove from 146mm to 60mm diameter
import math
rpm = 33 + 1/3
side_min = 22
groove_mm = math.pi * (146 + 60) / 2 * rpm * side_min / 1000  # meters approx
print(f"\nLP side spiral length ~ {groove_mm/1000:.1f} km of groove")
# RIAA time constants: 3180us, 318us, 75us
for t in (3180, 318, 75):
    print(f"RIAA {t}us -> corner {1/(2*math.pi*t*1e-6):.0f} Hz")
